answer.exemplar: A good answer separates the cost of one call from the number of calls, because the two statements are about different quantities and neither contradicts the other. Each activation does constant work, so the cost per call is indeed bounded, but a recursive walk performs one activation per node it visits and these activations are all alive at once, since a call cannot return until every call beneath it has returned. On a tree of depth d that is d simultaneous activations, each holding a frame of constant size, so the storage in use grows linearly in the depth and can exceed what the runtime reserves. An answer that only says the stack is too small has missed the point, and so has one that claims the per-call work must be quadratic; the fix is to change the shape of the computation, not the amount of work in a call. A good answer then offers a concrete redesign and checks that it is the same computation: convert the recursion into an explicit stack or queue that holds the pending nodes, which gives the same visit order under a last-in-first-out or first-in-first-out discipline and moves the memory demand from the call stack to a heap structure the programmer sizes; or, for a walk whose only purpose is to accumulate a quantity such as a sum or a count, replace the recursion with a running accumulator threaded through a loop or a fold, so the whole computation collapses to a fixed number of loop variables. The answer should note the trade-off honestly, since an explicit stack costs the same order of storage as the frames it replaces and is not free, and it should say that the change is safe only where the recomputation of results is independent, because turning recursion into iteration silently changes the order in which side effects happen when the routine is not a pure walk.

questions.explanation: This item rewards an answer that treats cost per call and the number of live calls as two separate quantities. The bound that matters is the product of the two, so a constant per-call cost multiplied by a number of simultaneous calls that grows with the depth of the input still grows without bound, and no amount of making each frame smaller removes the linear dependence. The stronger answer notices that a redesign only works when the computation has no order-dependent side effects, since an explicit stack reproduces a last-in-first-out discipline and an explicit queue reproduces a first-in-one, and a routine that both recurses and accumulates must choose which order it means.

answer.exemplar: A good answer builds a decision tree rather than analysing any particular procedure, because the bound is a statement about what any procedure can achieve. Each comparison of two keys has two outcomes, the left one is smaller or it is not, so a procedure that makes k comparisons is a binary tree of depth at most k with at most two to the k leaves. For the procedure to sort, every one of the n factorial arrangements of the keys must lead to a distinct leaf, because two arrangements that reach the same leaf have been told the same answers and are therefore indistinguishable to the procedure, and it would have to give them the same output and so be wrong on one of them. Hence n factorial cannot exceed two to the k, so k must be at least the base-two logarithm of n factorial, and Stirling's formula turns that into about n times the base-two logarithm of n. The assumption the argument depends on, and which a good answer names explicitly, is that the only source of information about the true order is these pairwise comparisons, so a procedure that may inspect the numeric values of the keys directly, or read them in a radix order, is not bound by it. answer.exemplar: A good answer separates the three requests and gives a structure and a cost for each, rather than naming a single structure and hoping it covers everything. A hash table suits the membership test, which resolves in expected constant time by computing a slot from the key and probing until it finds a match or an empty slot, and it suits insertion at the same expected cost, with the caveat that the load factor must be kept bounded because the cost of an unsuccessful search grows without limit as the table fills. The least recently added identifier is not a priority that a heap can express, because a heap can only compare keys and has no notion of insertion time, so the natural choice is a queue, and specifically a doubly linked list used as a queue, whose removal from the front is constant time. The best answer connects the two halves: a hash table from identifier to a node in the queue, plus the queue itself, gives constant expected time for both insertion and membership and constant time for the fetch, and deleting a node when it is processed is also constant time given the node's address, which is precisely what the table provides. It should also state the cost that was traded away, since a hash table does not support ordered traversal, so a request for the identifiers in sorted order would need a separate ordered structure or a different table entirely. A strong answer names a workload feature that would reverse the decision, and the best candidates are a requirement for ordered traversal, which rules out a plain hash table; a requirement for worst-case rather than expected time, which rules out hashing and points to a balanced tree at logarithmic cost per operation; or a workload in which the identifiers are small integers drawn from a bounded range, in which case a direct-address array of flags gives constant time with no collisions and less memory than a table with entries. A weak answer names one structure for all three requests without noticing that the fetch has a different requirement from the lookup, or gives cost claims with no mention of the expected versus worst-case distinction.

answer.exemplar: A good answer identifies the mechanism as memory locality rather than arithmetic effort, and makes the difference concrete in terms of addresses rather than in the abstract. Multiplying a whole row visits consecutive memory locations, so the processor fetches a cache line and the remaining entries on that line are already in the cache when the loop needs them. Multiplying a whole column strides through memory by a whole row length, so every single access lands on a different cache line and almost every fetch brings nothing that the next access can use. The number of multiplications is the same in both, and the number of instructions per multiplication is roughly the same, so the difference has to be in the cost of getting each operand to the arithmetic unit; with a row length much larger than a cache line the row-wise version can approach a many-fold speed-up even though the loop bodies are textually identical. The answer should then propose a measurement that tests the mechanism rather than the outcome, and the natural one is to vary the matrix dimension and check that the speed-up ratio changes in the way the explanation predicts, growing as the row length grows and flattening once the row fits in cache. Changing the row padding to break alignment, or running the same test on a machine with a much smaller cache, provides a second discriminating check, because if the explanation is right the two effects should move together. A strong answer also names the standard remedy, which is to restructure the column-wise loop into a blocked or tiled traversal so that each pass works on a submatrix small enough to stay resident, preserving the arithmetic exactly while changing only the order in which it is performed. A weak answer says only that caching is involved without saying what is being cached or why the pattern matters, or offers the timing comparison alone, which establishes a difference but cannot distinguish this explanation from any other, such as a difference in instruction count or in compiler optimisation.

questions.explanation: The item asks for a mechanism and a test, so a response that reports the two timings has answered only half of it. Marking rewards naming what is being reused between successive accesses, and rewards a measurement whose outcome could come out the other way if the explanation were wrong.

answer.exemplar: A good answer turns the amortised claim into a measurable prediction, because the claim is about an average over a whole sequence of operations rather than about any single one, and an experiment that times one append cannot test it. The prediction to test is that if n items are appended to an array that starts with capacity one and doubles whenever it fills, then the total time for the whole sequence grows no faster than a fixed multiple of n, so the cost per append plotted against n should flatten towards a horizontal line. The design should therefore run the sequence for a geometric ladder of sizes, for example ten, a hundred, ten thousand and a million appends, timing the whole sequence rather than any individual append, and repeating each size many times to get a stable central estimate. It should record both the total time and the number of copies, and it should note that the very first append after each doubling is expected to be individually slow, so any instrumentation that times single appends will see spikes and must average over the sequence or report a distribution. The crucial addition is the stated refutation criterion, and it should be a quantitative one: if the measured cost per append grows without bound as n increases, or if the total time for a sequence of n appends is observed to scale faster than linearly, the claim is refuted, and in particular a total that scales as n squared would be the signature of copying on every append rather than on a geometric schedule. A strong answer also says what would be controlled, such as running each size in a fresh process so that the heap state from the previous size cannot bias the next, and warming up before the first timed run so that the cost of the very first call is not attributed to the algorithm. A weak answer times a single append at one size and concludes from it, which cannot distinguish a constant amortised cost from a constant true cost, and a weaker answer omits the refutation criterion entirely, so the experiment is incapable of disagreeing with the claim.

answer.exemplar: A complete answer has three parts and must be explicit about which quantity is being generalised. The statement to prove is that for every integer n at least one, the sum of the odd numbers from one to the term two n minus one equals n squared. The base case takes n equal to one, where the sum is a single term, one, and one squared is also one, so the statement holds at the first value. The inductive hypothesis then assumes the statement holds for some particular integer k, that is that one plus three plus five and so on up to two k minus one equals k squared, and the inductive step must show that the statement holds at k plus one, where the new sum has one more term, namely two k plus one, so the sum becomes k squared plus two k plus one, which is exactly the square of k plus one, and the step closes. An answer that only checks a few small cases has verified the identity numerically without proving it, and a weak answer states the hypothesis without using it in the step, which is the most common failure. A strong answer also notes why the identity is a statement about odd numbers specifically, since the extra term on passing from k to k plus one is two k plus one, and that is the whole content of the step. A polished answer may remark that the two sides can also be seen as the areas of nested squares, which explains why the identity is true as well as proving it, and may comment that the induction would fail if the step were attempted with the even numbers, where the corresponding claim does not hold.

questions.explanation: Counting all two-to-the-four subsets gives sixteen, but that counts duplicates, because the two occurrences of a and the two of b are interchangeable. Building the set of distinct subsequences one character at a time gives one after a, two after b, four after a again, since the new a reproduces four sequences already present, and twelve after the final b, which contributes eight new ones and reproduces four. Two independent computations agree, an explicit construction of the set and a running dynamic program that doubles the count and subtracts the count at the position of the previous occurrence of the same character. The answer sixteen is the count with no duplicates removed, and eight is what the count would be if the second copy of each letter were ignored, as it would be in a string with four distinct characters.

questions.explanation: A binary heap stores only the relation that a parent outranks its children, and that is enough to find the extreme element at the root and to restore the relation along one path after an update, which is why both operations cost the height of the tree, that is, the base-two logarithm of the number of elements. A sorted array gives constant-time access to the extreme but pays a linear cost to insert, because the remaining elements must shift. Neither structure supports both cheaply, and the heap's real cost is not memory but order: from a heap one cannot list the jobs from highest to lowest without removing them one at a time, whereas a sorted array can. A program that needs occasional ordered reporting may prefer the array, and one that only adds and takes should prefer the heap; the claim of dominance in the third option is false precisely because the ordered walk is exactly what the heap does not give.
questions.hint: Ask which operations the workload actually performs often, and what each structure makes expensive.
questions.learningObjective: compare a heap-backed and an array-backed priority queue

questions.explanation: A spanning tree on eight vertices keeps seven edges, so thirteen minus seven is six edges beyond the tree, and those six are the independent cycles, since removing any one of them leaves a graph with one fewer cycle. The total degree is the sum of all vertex degrees, and since each of the thirteen edges contributes one to the degree of each of its two endpoints, the total is twenty-six. Two independent routes agree, doubling the edge count directly and adding the degrees of a concrete graph with the given vertex and edge counts, whose degrees sum to twenty-six. The distinction between the two numbers in the item is the point: six is a count of edges and twenty-six is a count of incidences, and confusing them is the common error.

answer.exemplar: A good answer starts from the observation that algorithms differ in how much work they do on a nearly ordered input as against a random one, and that adaptivity is the property of exploiting that difference. What it buys is speed on the inputs that occur in practice, since real data is often close to ordered: a data set that receives a few small updates a day can be resorted by an adaptive procedure for far less work than a fresh sort would cost, and the same is true of merging two long runs that are each already sorted. The reason it is not free is that the procedure has to notice, which means comparing elements that a non-adaptive method would not have compared; a method achieves the property precisely by performing comparisons whose outcomes are discarded when the input is random, so on a random input an adaptive procedure does strictly more work than a non-adaptive one of the same average cost. That is the trade, and a good answer states it as a trade rather than as a free improvement. The merge sort is not adaptive because it never looks at the order of the input: it splits the list by position, sorts each half independently and merges by comparing fronts, and the comparisons it makes are entirely determined by the two halves rather than by the arrangement of the values, so a nearly sorted input costs exactly the same as a random one. A strong answer gives the contrasting case, since insertion sort is adaptive, performing one comparison per element on an already sorted list and the full quadratic number on a random one, and it may note that timsort-style methods achieve adaptivity by first identifying sorted runs and merging only those, which is adaptivity assembled from two non-adaptive pieces. A weak answer defines the term without saying what it is worth, or claims a merge sort is adaptive because it examines all of its elements, which confuses touching the data with responding to its order.

questions.explanation: The item rewards an answer that states the benefit, the price in comparisons wasted on random input, and a mechanism-based reason why a merge sort cannot benefit, and it penalises an answer that asserts adaptivity without pricing it.
